title: Sudden and gradual
hookLine: schools stress sudden awakening or gradual training, and some hold both together

cards: Two verses are pinned to a monastery wall in old China, so the story goes. The abbot is choosing an heir, and has asked his monks to write down what they understand.

The senior monk writes that the mind is like a bright mirror, and the work is to wipe it, again and again, so no dust can settle. People nod. Then a kitchen worker who cannot read asks someone to write a reply for him.
The mirror, he says, was never a thing to begin with. So where would the dust land? One verse is about patient cleaning.
The other is about seeing all at once.

teach.b: That story comes from the Platform Sutra, which tells it about the senior monk Shenxiu and the kitchen worker Huineng.

Chan tradition later spoke of a southern school that stressed sudden awakening and a northern school that stressed gradual training. The two words stuck. Now go back to the Pali texts, and both are already there.
In one discourse, the Buddha compares his teaching to the great ocean, whose floor slopes down little by little, with no sudden cliff.
So too the training is gradual, step by step; knowledge does not come in an abrupt leap.
Then there is Bahiya of the bark cloth. He finds the Buddha on his alms round in the street and will not wait.

The Buddha gives him a teaching of a few lines: in the seen, let there be only the seen; in the heard, only the heard. And right there, the text says, Bahiya's mind is freed. No years of training on the page.
Just a street, and a sentence. So which is it? Some teachers would say the question is the wrong shape.
The Korean teacher Chinul taught sudden awakening followed by gradual cultivation: you may see clearly in one moment, then spend years letting your habits catch up.
Ice may be seen to be water at once, and still take time to melt.
Zen halls tell stories of breakthroughs; Theravada teachers map the path in stages, as the ocean simile does. Each keeps the other side somewhere in its house.

how: Some Zen and Chan schools speak of sudden awakening and tell stories of breakthrough moments; Theravada teachers often describe a gradual training in stages; and teachers such as the Korean master Chinul taught sudden awakening followed by gradual cultivation.

o: awakening seen in a flash, or grown by steady training
two speeds of chanting, quick at dawn and slow at night
two Zen schools that split apart and never spoke again

games.q: you're Bahiya. you've found the Buddha on his alms round in the street. what do you do?
o: wait politely until he's back at the monastery.
ask him to teach you, right there, now.
join the monks and start years of training first.
games.why: Bahiya won't wait. the Buddha teaches him in the street: in the seen, only the seen. and the text says his mind is freed right there.

practice: Call up one insight that came suddenly, a moment when something just clicked, and stay with it for a few breaths. Then call up one that came slowly, a patience built over years, a habit that took countless small tries.
One opened a door; the other walked you through it.

wordCard.voice: Sudden and gradual. Two ways schools describe awakening: seen in a flash, or grown by steady training, and often both, one after the other. Today's word.

orig.note: Chinese dunwu: sudden awakening, the word Chan schools used for seeing all at once.

carryVoice: Your line: both are true. The week closes: one Buddha or many, Buddha-nature, emptiness, rebirth, lay and monastic, devotion and meditation, and sudden and gradual. A full week, done.
